title: Chapter 3: Critical Sections — Where & When?
description: Diagnosing when shared global variables require mutual exclusion: atomic vs. compound writes, structs, read-modify-write (var++), floats/doubles, std::vector<bool>, and multi-core cache hazards.

sections.title: 1. Analyzing Concurrent Access Scenarios (Single-Core)
sections.description: Evaluating when data corruption can occur on a single-core CPU.

blocks.title: What Are We Protecting Against?
blocks.content:
In `PCO_3_sectioncritique.pdf`, we examine **12 concrete C++ scenarios** on a **single-core CPU** (*processeur simple cœur*), asking:

> *Is mutual exclusion required to avoid **data corruption** or **broken behavior** (ignoring instruction ordering)?*

### Category A: Simple `int` Writes & Reads (Slides 5–6, 13)
* **Case 1:** `TacheA: var = a;` and `TacheB: var = b;` (`static int var;`). On a 32-bit/64-bit CPU, a single aligned `int` store is one machine instruction—`var` ends up holding either `a` or `b` (never half-`a`, half-`b`).
* **Case 2:** `taskA: var = a;` and `taskB: b = var;`. Similarly, `b` reads either the old or new `var`.

### Category B: Compound Data & Read-Modify-Write (Slides 7–12)
* **Case 3 & 4 (`struct_t var` with `var.a`, `var.b`):** Writing/reading two fields is **not atomic**! A context switch between `var.a = a` and `var.b = b` causes **torn structs** (mixing `TacheA`'s `a` with `TacheB`'s `b`). **Needs mutual exclusion!**
* **Case 5 (`var++` vs `var++`):** `var++` compiles to 3 instructions (`load`, `add 1`, `store`). Interleaving loses updates! **Needs mutual exclusion!**
* **Case 6 (`var++` vs `b = var`):** `b` reads a valid integer (before or after increment), though in C++ a data race is still Undefined Behavior.
* **Case 7 (`TacheA: var++`, `TacheB: var++`, `TacheC: c = var`):** Both `var++` tasks corrupt each other -> **Needs mutual exclusion!**
* **Case 8 (`taskA: var++`, `taskB: if (b > 10) var = 0; else var++;`):** Both modify `var` non-atomically -> **Needs mutual exclusion!**

blocks.title: Hidden Non-Atomic Traps: `double` & `std::vector<bool>`
blocks.content:
Even seemingly innocent single-line assignments can corrupt data on a single core:

| Scenario | Safe on 32-bit Single-Core? | Why? |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| `static float var;` (`var = a` / `var = b`) | Depends on arch (usually 32-bit) | A 32-bit `float` fits in a single 32-bit bus transfer. |
| `static double var;` (`var = a` / `var = b`) | **NO (on 32-bit CPU)** | A 64-bit `double` requires **two** 32-bit memory writes! A preemption mid-write produces a **corrupted half-old, half-new `double`**. |
| `std::vector<bool> vec;` (`vec[0] = a` / `vec[1] = b` or `vec[0] = b`) | **NO** | `std::vector<bool>` packs 8 booleans into **1 byte** (bitfield)! Modifying `vec[0]` performs a **read-modify-write** on the entire byte, clobbering adjacent bits! |

blocks.title: Why std::vector<bool> Causes Data Races
blocks.caption: Even writing to DIFFERENT indices (vec[0] and vec[1]) in std::vector<bool> is a race condition because both share the same underlying byte.

  TB["Thread B: vec[1] = true\n1. Read byte\n2. Set bit 1\n3. Write byte"]

sections.title: 2. Multi-Core Caches & The Golden Rule
sections.description: Why single-core assumptions collapse on multi-core hardware.

blocks.title: Multi-Core Processors & Cache Coherency
blocks.content:
Even if an operation looks single-instruction on a single core, **modern processors are multi-core**:

* **Private Core Caches:** Each CPU core has its own local L1/L2 cache.
* **No Automatic Sync Without Synchronization:** Nothing forces cores to immediately flush/synchronize caches unless explicit synchronization primitives (mutexes, atomics, memory barriers) are used.
* **C++ Standard:** Concurrent unsynchronized read/write (or write/write) to the same memory location is a **Data Race = Undefined Behavior**.

> [!CAUTION]
> **The Golden Rule of PCO (Slide 17):**
> *"Dans le doute... **Protégez tous les accès concurrents !**"* (When in doubt, protect **all** concurrent accesses!)

blocks.question: Why can `static double var; var = a;` (executed concurrently by two threads) corrupt `var` on a 32-bit single-core CPU?
options: A 64-bit `double` requires two 32-bit memory writes, so a context switch between them produces a torn value.
Floating-point registers are shared across all threads in the same process.
C++ `double` variables are always stored on the stack, not in the data segment.
A `double` cannot be stored in a global variable.
blocks.correct_answer: A 64-bit `double` requires two 32-bit memory writes, so a context switch between them produces a torn value.
blocks.explanation: On a 32-bit architecture, writing a 64-bit `double` takes two separate 32-bit store instructions. If a preemption occurs between the first and second store, `var` ends up with 32 bits from Thread A and 32 bits from Thread B (a torn, corrupted floating-point value).
hints: How many bits wide is a `double` compared to a 32-bit CPU bus?
What happens if a context switch occurs halfway through writing a 64-bit value?

blocks.question: Why is concurrent modification of `std::vector<bool>` dangerous even when Thread A only writes `vec[0]` and Thread B only writes `vec[1]`?
options: `std::vector<bool>` packs multiple booleans as bits inside the same byte, requiring a non-atomic read-modify-write of that byte.
`std::vector<bool>` allocates each boolean on a separate heap page.
blocks.correct_answer: `std::vector<bool>` packs multiple booleans as bits inside the same byte, requiring a non-atomic read-modify-write of that byte.
blocks.explanation: `std::vector<bool>` is a space-optimized specialization that stores 8 booleans per byte. Setting `vec[0]` reads the whole byte, flips bit 0, and writes the whole byte back—potentially overwriting Thread B's concurrent update to bit 1 (`vec[1]`).
hints: How does `std::vector<bool>` optimize memory usage in C++?
Can a CPU write a single bit in RAM without reading and writing the surrounding byte?
